reply.text: `==` tests whether two objects have equal values, calling the `__eq__` method, while `is` tests whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory, comparing identity (effectively `id(a) == id(b)`). Two equal values can be distinct objects, so `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is `True` but `[1, 2] is [1, 2]` is `False`. Use `==` for value comparison, and reserve `is` for identity checks, most commonly `x is None`, since `None` is a singleton. Avoid `is` for numbers and strings: CPython caches some small integers and interns some strings, so `is` may seem to work by accident, and it can give different results across implementations.
